title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback for open-ended mathematics responses. The authors compare three approaches: a fine-tuned open-source LLM called GOAT (based on Mistral), a prior similarity-based method called SBERT-Canberra, and GPT-4 used in a zero-shot prompting setup. The study asks how well these systems predict teacher-assigned scores and how well they generate feedback judged by human teachers.

The data come from an online learning platform using Illustrative Mathematics-style open-response problems. The dataset includes responses from approximately 50 teachers’ classrooms, restricted to language-based questions, and focuses on middle-school math problems. The models were trained and tested on 50 problems with 5,000 total student responses, with 100 additional responses sampled for teacher review of feedback quality. Two teachers with prior teaching experience evaluated generated feedback for accuracy, relevancy, motivation, and preference.

Results show that GOAT outperformed SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on scoring metrics, but GPT-4 produced feedback that teachers judged to be more accurate, more relevant, less demotivating, and more preferred overall. The authors conclude that task-specific fine-tuning can improve auto-scoring, while a strong general-purpose LLM may still be better for high-quality feedback generation. They also note that teacher-provided feedback in the training data was often vague or inconsistent, which likely limited performance.

identified_tools.name: Mistral
identified_tools.description: An open-source large language model family used for text generation and downstream fine-tuning.
identified_tools.use_case: Fine-tuned (as GOAT) on student open-ended math responses and teacher-provided scores/feedback to generate automated scores and feedback; also compared against SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 Turbo.

findings.finding_summary: On the scoring task, the fine-tuned Mistral-based GOAT model outperformed SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on all three reported metrics. Reported results were AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, and Kappa=0.422 on the test set (n=1,000 student responses).
findings.measure: Teacher score prediction on open-ended math responses

findings.finding_summary: For feedback generation, GOAT was rated by two teachers as 68% accurate, 88% relevant, 48% motivating, and 5% demotivating, and was selected as the preferred feedback 12% of the time on average. The same qualitative evaluation used 100 sampled test responses (n=100). GPT-4 was preferred more often, but GOAT was judged substantially better than SBERT-Canberra on accuracy and relevance.
findings.measure: Human ratings of feedback accuracy, relevance, motivation, demotivation, and preference

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used for text generation and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied via the GPT-4 Turbo model in zero-shot mode to score student open-ended math responses and generate feedback; compared with GOAT and SBERT-Canberra.

findings.finding_summary: On scoring open-ended math responses, GPT-4 Turbo underperformed the fine-tuned GOAT model and SBERT-Canberra on AUC and Kappa, though its RMSE was intermediate. Reported results were AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.16, and Kappa=0.266 on n=1,000 test responses.
findings.measure: Teacher score prediction on open-ended math responses

findings.finding_summary: For feedback generation, GPT-4 was rated highest by two human evaluators: 86% consensus accuracy, 91% consensus relevance, 52% consensus motivation, 1% consensus demotivation, and 77.5% average preference. The qualitative review used 100 sampled test responses (n=100), and GPT-4 was preferred over GOAT and SBERT-Canberra.
findings.measure: Human ratings of feedback accuracy, relevance, motivation, demotivation, and preference

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single comparative study with a test-train split and small human-rater component, not a randomized trial or meta-analysis. It provides useful empirical evidence, but the methodology and reporting leave some concerns, so yellow is most appropriate.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear performance differences, but no standardized educational effect sizes are provided, and the outcomes are technical model metrics rather than classroom learning gains. The practical impact is promising but currently modest and uncertain for teacher practice.
